catalog_quote: 2.3.5 Stress. Generally, the lexical roots of Kilen are stressed on the first syllable, as shown below in (71): (71a) ˈəli 'more' (71b) dˈubə 'sharp' (71c) sˈəfəɾə- 'hold'. A secondary stress will be involved when a word contains four syllables or more, as in the situations illustrated below: A. Compound words: the secondary stress falls on the first syllable of the last polysyllabic component of the entire compound as shown in (72) (72) sˈɔxunsˌɔjan / sˈɔxun-sˌɔjan / light.bright yellow-yellow / dark yellow. B. Inflected forms: the secondary stress falls on the first syllable of a inflected suffix chain containing more than one syllable; and the stem must be a polysyllabic word, as shown in (73): (73) dʑˈfə-xˌəi-mi / eat-PERF-1SG / I have eaten. [p. 41] ... Generally, centralization in Kilen takes place in all unstressed vowels (Kilen lexical stress mostly falls on the initial syllable.) [p. 25] ... In Kilen, compounds are stressed on the first syllable of the first element; there is no second stress in the whole compound word [p. 52]

A. Compound words: the secondary stress falls on the first syllable of the last polysyllabic component of the entire compound a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the first syllable of the lexical root (and, in compounds, on the first syllable of the first element). Words of four or more syllables get a secondary stress: in compounds on the first syllable of the last polysyllabic member, in inflected words on the first syllable of a polysyllabic suffix chain attached to a polysyllabic stem. Unstressed vowels centralize (p. 20).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, explicit: only in words of 4+ syllables; compound: first syllable of the last polysyllabic component; inflected form: first syllable of a multi-syllable suffix chain after a polysyllabic stem (examples 72-73). Elsewhere (p. 52) the author says a compound 'has just one stress.. there is no second stress in the whole compound word', which sits uneasily with example (72).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'Generally' and (p. 20) 'mostly falls on the initial syllable'; p. 14 notes a Manchu-influenced 'suffix-splitting' in which case suffixes detach from the stem and bear 'full stress'. The stress marks in (71b-c) are printed after the onset consonant (dˈubə, sˈəfəɾə-), i.e. still the first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical roots, compounds, inflected words); IPA citation forms from the author's own fieldwork/consultation with the last fluent speakers (Wu Mingxiang) plus earlier Chinese descriptions; no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Zhang 2013 describes the Kilen (Qileng 奇楞) variety of Hezhe spoken around Jiejinkou, Tongjiang, eastern Heilongjiang (consultant Wu Mingxiang), which is exactly Glottolog kile1243 (alt. names Hezhen, 赫哲語奇楞方言). Zhang distinguishes it from the other Chinese Hezhe dialect he calls 'Hezhen/Ezhen' (Udihe-like). The Russian-side Kur-Urmi/Kili of Sunik 1958 is grouped under the same glottocode by Glottolog but is not covered by the quoted statement.
